To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mineralocorticoid receptors antagonists (MRAS) are associated with significant improvement of diastolic dysfunction and markers of cardiac remodeling in patients with asymptotic diastolic dysfunction.

mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) are expressed on cardiac myocytes and fibroblasts, that aldosterone is an endogenous ligand for MR, that activation of MR is detrimental to the heart in the context of diastolic dysfunction, that inhibition of MR with spironolactone and eplerenone improves cardiac function, that the beneficial effects of MR inhibition are independent of blood pressure, that the effects of MR inhibition on cardiac fibrosis are independent of changes in blood pressure,
mineralocorticoid receptors are important mediators of cardiac fibrosis and remodeling in heart failure with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of mineralocorticoids on the cardiovascular system.
the effects of mineralocorticoids and their antagonists on the heart and the cardiovascular system in general.
the effects of mineralocorticoids on the heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MRA therapy in diastolic heart failure and HFPEF is safe and associated with significant improvement diastolic function.
MRAs may improve diastolic function in patients with HFPEF, but this needs further study.
MRA use in patients with diatolic dysfunction or HFpEF is associated with significant improvements in diastolic and systolic function and markers for myocardial collagen turnover.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone) improve diastolic function in patients with heart disease.
mineralocorticoid antagonists improve diastolic function in patients with diatolic dysfunction and HFpEF without affecting LV mass.
MRAs have a favorable effect on LV structure and diastolic function in patients with diatolic dysfunction or HFpEF, but the effect on LV systolic function is less clear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mineralocorticoid receptors are important in the pathogenesis of diastolic dysfunction and heart failure with preserved systolic function.
MRA therapy is associated with significant reduction of diastolic dysfunction in patients with asymptotic diastolic dysfunction.
MRAs have an effect on diastolic function that is not mediated by changes in LV mass or geometry.
